sections.title: Organization and internal balance
sections.text:
Human physiology explains how the body functions. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs cooperate in systems. Homeostasis maintains internal variables within workable ranges despite changing external conditions. Negative feedback counteracts a deviation: a sensor detects change, a coordinating system compares it with relevant requirements and effectors alter the variable. Body-temperature and glucose regulation illustrate this pattern.

Positive feedback amplifies a process until an endpoint is reached, as in coordinated uterine contractions during childbirth. It is not the main stabilizing mechanism for most internal conditions. A reference range also does not mean one exact value remains unchanged throughout the day; physiological variables depend on activity, timing and health.

sections.title: Digestion and absorption
sections.text:
Digestion breaks food into absorbable components. Chewing mechanically reduces food, while salivary amylase begins starch hydrolysis. Swallowing moves a bolus through the oesophagus by coordinated muscular contractions called peristalsis. The stomach mixes food, secretes acid and begins substantial protein digestion through pepsin. Acid also contributes to defence against many ingested organisms.

The small intestine is the main site of digestion and nutrient absorption. Pancreatic enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Bicarbonate helps neutralize acidic stomach contents. Bile, made by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, emulsifies fat and supports delivery of lipid products to the absorptive surface; it is not itself a digestive enzyme.

Villi and microvilli provide a large absorptive area. Sugars and amino acids enter blood through appropriate transport proteins and usually travel first to the liver through portal circulation. Many long-chain lipid products are reassembled and packaged into chylomicrons, which initially enter lymph. The large intestine recovers water and electrolytes and supports microbial fermentation. Defecation removes unabsorbed material; it differs from renal excretion of metabolic wastes.

sections.title: Breathing, gas exchange and circulation
sections.text:
During inhalation, contraction of the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles expands the thoracic cavity. Pressure falls relative to outside air and air enters. Relaxed exhalation is mainly driven by elastic recoil. Ventilation moves air; gas exchange transfers oxygen and carbon dioxide across respiratory surfaces; cellular respiration uses fuels to generate ATP. These are connected but distinct processes.

Alveoli provide thin, moist surfaces beside capillaries. Oxygen diffuses into blood down its partial-pressure gradient, while carbon dioxide diffuses toward alveolar air. Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries most oxygen. Higher carbon dioxide and lower pH in active tissues can lower haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, helping unloading through the Bohr effect. Most carbon dioxide is carried after conversion into bicarbonate, with additional dissolved and protein-bound fractions.

The right side of the heart pumps blood toward the lungs; the left side pumps it through systemic circulation. Valves promote one-way flow. The sinoatrial node usually initiates the normal rhythm, and the conduction system coordinates contraction. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins toward it; their names describe direction, not oxygen content. Pulmonary arteries normally carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

```text
Body tissues → veins → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries
→ lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → tissues
```

Capillaries permit exchange with tissues. Plasma transports dissolved substances; red cells carry respiratory gases; white cells contribute to defence; platelets help haemostasis. Lymphatic vessels return excess tissue fluid and transport some absorbed lipids. They also connect tissue surveillance with immune responses.

sections.title: Kidneys and fluid balance
sections.text:
The kidneys regulate water, electrolytes, acid–base conditions and waste excretion. Their functional units are nephrons. Filtration at the glomerulus moves water and small solutes from blood into the initial filtrate, while blood cells and most large proteins are retained. Tubular reabsorption retrieves needed substances; secretion adds selected substances from blood to tubular fluid. Final urine composition reflects all three processes.

Glucose is normally filtered and then efficiently reabsorbed, mainly in the proximal tubule, at usual blood concentrations. Its absence from final urine does not mean the glomerulus never filtered it. The loop of Henle and associated medullary arrangement help establish gradients used for urine concentration.

Antidiuretic hormone, ADH, promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels in collecting-duct principal cells, increasing water permeability and conservation under suitable conditions. Aldosterone influences sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Kidney regulation depends on blood flow, hormones and cellular transport, so drinking more water does not automatically correct every disturbance of body chemistry.

sections.title: Nervous and endocrine coordination
sections.text:
Neurons communicate using electrical signals and chemical synapses. A resting membrane potential depends on ion gradients and selective permeability. In many neurons, an action potential begins with voltage-gated sodium channels opening and sodium entering, followed by processes including potassium efflux that restore membrane voltage. The sodium–potassium pump maintains the underlying gradients over time; it does not directly produce each rapid depolarizing upstroke.

At a typical chemical synapse, arrival of an action potential opens calcium channels. Calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release. Transmitter binds to receptors on the next cell and changes its behaviour. Myelin increases conduction efficiency by allowing action potentials to regenerate mainly at gaps called nodes. Reflex arcs can coordinate rapid responses before conscious processing is complete.

Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood. Target cells respond because they possess appropriate receptors. Insulin from pancreatic beta cells promotes nutrient storage and glucose uptake in several insulin-sensitive tissues. Glucagon from alpha cells supports glucose availability during fasting, especially through liver metabolism. Not every tissue requires insulin stimulation for glucose entry.

Thyroid hormones influence metabolism and development; parathyroid hormone supports calcium homeostasis through bone, kidney and vitamin-D-related pathways. Adrenal hormones contribute to stress responses and salt regulation. Nervous and endocrine systems interact, and hormonal effects are not invariably slow while neural effects are not invariably brief.

sections.title: Movement, reproduction and immunity
sections.text:
Bones support the body, protect organs, store minerals and contain marrow involved in blood-cell production. Skeletal muscles contract through interactions between actin and myosin regulated by calcium and powered by ATP. Tendons connect muscles to bones; ligaments connect bones at joints. Smooth and cardiac muscles have distinct control and structural properties.

Human reproduction involves gametes formed through meiosis. Fertilization usually occurs in the uterine tube, producing a zygote that divides and can implant in the uterus. The placenta supports exchange between maternal and developing fetal systems without normal unrestricted mixing of their blood. Hormonal feedback regulates gamete production and the menstrual cycle. Reproduction depends on coordinated anatomy, endocrine control and cellular development.

Innate immunity includes barriers, inflammation, phagocytic cells and other rapid defences. Adaptive immunity includes antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes. B-cell descendants can produce antibodies; T cells support coordination or eliminate selected infected cells. Memory cells can produce faster responses on later exposure. Antibodies are not antibiotics, and inflammation is not proof that every illness is bacterial.

Immune function also distinguishes infection, allergy and autoimmunity. Infection involves a pathogen; allergy is an inappropriate response to a usually harmless antigen; autoimmunity targets self-components. Vaccination uses immune learning to reduce future disease risk, as developed in Chapter 13.

**Digestive regulation and liver function.** The liver processes absorbed nutrients, stores glycogen, produces bile and synthesizes important plasma proteins. It also transforms many compounds for further use or elimination. Detoxification is not a single process that makes every harmful substance harmless: some reactions can produce reactive intermediates, and capacity can be exceeded. Digestive hormones and nerve signals coordinate secretion and movement so that food receives the appropriate processing at each stage.

**Why lung structure supports diffusion.** Effective gas exchange requires a large surface, a short diffusion distance and maintained partial-pressure gradients. Alveolar walls and adjacent capillaries provide a thin barrier, while ventilation renews air and perfusion renews blood. Surfactant reduces surface tension and helps prevent small alveoli from collapsing. Failure of ventilation, thickening of the barrier or reduced blood flow can impair exchange through different mechanisms even if the measured oxygen content of outside air is normal.

**The cardiac cycle and blood pressure.** During filling, relaxed chambers receive blood. Atrial contraction contributes to ventricular filling, ventricular contraction raises pressure and the outflow valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds the relevant arterial pressure. Valve closure prevents substantial backflow as pressure relationships change. Systolic pressure refers to the higher arterial pressure associated with ventricular ejection; diastolic pressure is the lower pressure between beats. Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and vascular resistance, while elastic arteries smooth the pulsatile flow.

**Clotting and oxygen delivery.** Platelets adhere and activate at an injury, and a cascade of coagulation reactions generates a fibrin network that stabilizes the plug. This protects against blood loss, but inappropriate clot formation can obstruct circulation. Oxygen delivery depends on blood flow and blood oxygen content, not merely breathing rate. Anaemia can reduce delivery by lowering oxygen-carrying capacity even when the lungs exchange gases effectively.

**Kidney filtration is not simple sieving of all wastes.** Small useful substances such as glucose enter the filtrate along with waste-related solutes. Tubules then recover needed material using selective transport, while secretion adds other substances. The amount excreted can be expressed conceptually as filtered amount minus reabsorbed amount plus secreted amount. Hormonal regulation changes these fluxes according to body needs. A large urine volume can result from different causes and does not automatically establish effective removal of every harmful substance.

**Temperature regulation as a feedback example.** Thermal information reaches coordinating centres, and responses can include changes in skin blood flow, sweating, behaviour and muscle activity. Evaporating sweat removes heat, but high humidity limits evaporative cooling. In cold conditions, reduced skin blood flow limits heat transfer and shivering increases metabolic heat production. Core temperature is maintained through several interacting mechanisms, so air temperature alone cannot predict physiological heat stress.

**Endocrine feedback and receptor specificity.** The hypothalamus and pituitary participate in hormonal control axes. A peripheral hormone can feed back to reduce earlier stimulating signals. Target tissues respond according to their receptors and intracellular machinery, which is why the same circulating hormone can have different effects in different tissues. Hormone concentration, receptor sensitivity and timing all influence response; a gland's name alone does not explain the physiological effect.

**Immune coordination and memory.** Antigen-presenting cells help connect early recognition with adaptive responses. Helper T cells support other immune activities, cytotoxic T cells can eliminate selected infected cells and antibody-producing cells release molecules that bind specific targets. Antibodies can neutralize a pathogen or mark it for other mechanisms; they do not always kill an organism directly. Memory responses depend on the antigen and immune history and are not an unlimited shield against every subsequent infection.

**Integration during exercise.** Active muscles consume more ATP, increasing demand for oxygen and fuels and producing more carbon dioxide and heat. Ventilation and cardiac output rise, blood flow is redistributed and temperature-regulation mechanisms respond. Nervous signals act rapidly while hormonal changes help mobilize energy stores. This example connects respiratory, circulatory, muscular, endocrine and excretory functions and shows why human physiology is best understood as coordinated systems rather than separate lists of organs.

questions.prompt: At the beginning of a typical neuronal action potential, which membrane event drives the rapid depolarizing upstroke?

options.A: Complete shutdown of all ion movement
options.B: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels and inward sodium current

questions.explanation: Voltage-gated Na+ channels create the rapid inward current associated with the upstroke of many neuronal action potentials.

questions.prompt: A healthy nephron filters glucose into the initial filtrate. Why is glucose usually absent from normal final urine at physiologically typical blood concentrations?

options.B: Glucose never crosses the filtration barrier under any circumstance
options.C: It is normally reabsorbed efficiently, mainly in the proximal tubule

questions.explanation: Filtered glucose is normally reclaimed by tubular transporters, primarily in the proximal tubule.

questions.prompt: ADH increases water conservation partly by promoting which change in kidney collecting-duct principal cells?

options.C: Permanent closure of every blood vessel
options.D: Insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane

questions.explanation: ADH signaling promotes aquaporin-2 availability at the apical membrane, increasing water permeability.

questions.prompt: Why does oxygen normally move from alveolar air into pulmonary capillary blood?

options.A: Blood produces a stronger gravity field
options.B: An oxygen partial-pressure gradient supports diffusion
options.C: The diaphragm chemically attracts all oxygen atoms
options.D: Hemoglobin pumps air directly into arteries

questions.explanation: Gas transfer occurs across the thin respiratory membrane according to partial-pressure gradients and diffusion conditions.

questions.prompt: Which cardiac structure normally initiates the rhythmic electrical activity of a healthy adult heart?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node contains pacemaker cells that usually initiate the heartbeat.

questions.prompt: In actively metabolizing tissues, elevated CO₂ and lower pH can promote which hemoglobin response?

options.A: Reduced oxygen affinity and greater oxygen unloading
options.B: Complete conversion of hemoglobin into iron ore

questions.explanation: The Bohr effect reduces hemoglobin's oxygen affinity under higher CO₂/lower-pH conditions, facilitating tissue oxygen delivery.

questions.prompt: At a typical chemical synapse, calcium influx into a presynaptic terminal most directly promotes:

options.B: Conversion of the neuron into a bacterium
options.C: Instant loss of every neurotransmitter receptor
options.D: Fusion of synaptic vesicles and neurotransmitter release

questions.explanation: Voltage-gated calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion machinery, allowing neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft.

questions.prompt: Parathyroid hormone is important for calcium homeostasis because it can:

options.B: Promote mechanisms that increase blood calcium concentration

questions.explanation: PTH influences bone, kidney and vitamin-D-related pathways to regulate extracellular calcium.
